n0001.title: Replication Crisis
n0001.gist: Science's results often fail to repeat because of weak statistics, biased publishing, and career pressures, prompting reforms to restore trust.
n0001.question: Replication crisis — why do so many published findings fail to replicate, and what can fix it? (a survey and reform agenda)

n0002.title: Definitions and Background
n0002.gist: Replication means re-running a study with new data to check a result, and whether a finding counts as supported depends on statistical significance tests whose logic this section lays out.
n0002.question: Replication crisis — what do key terms like replication, significance, and power actually mean? (a glossary)

n0003.title: Overview of the Crisis
n0003.gist: Widespread failure to reproduce published results, most visible in psychology and medicine, has spread across sciences and given rise to a new field, metascience, that studies research practice itself.

n0010.title: Types of Replication
n0010.gist: Researchers separate reproducibility, rerunning the same data, from replication, repeating a study with new data, and distinguish direct, systematic, and conceptual replication types.

n0020.title: Statistical Significance Basics
n0020.gist: A result counts as supported when it crosses a preset probability threshold, the p-value, which is routinely misunderstood even though it only estimates the chance of a false positive.

n0024.title: Null Hypothesis Testing Framework
n0024.gist: A null-hypothesis test compares a measured effect to a threshold and can go wrong in four ways, producing false positives or false negatives depending on sample and effect size.

n0035.title: Significance, Power, and P-values
n0035.gist: The chance a test wrongly rejects a true null hypothesis is the significance level, while the chance it correctly detects a real effect is called statistical power, and together they set how trustworthy any single p-value is.

n0042.title: History of the Crisis
n0042.gist: A cluster of failed replications in the early 2010s, from social priming to cancer biology, triggered the label 'replication crisis,' though concerns about weak replication stretch back decades.
n0042.question: Replication crisis — how and when did the crisis become visible, and was it really new? (a historical account)

n0043.title: Precursors to the Crisis
n0043.gist: Four episodes, failed social-priming replications, discredited ESP studies, dismal biomedical replication rates, and new p-hacking research, together sparked a 'crisis of confidence' across fields.

n0049.title: Emergence of the Term
n0049.gist: The label 'replication crisis' arose in the early 2010s, but scholars note that similar worries about weak replication and biased publishing were already voiced from the 1960s onward.

n0054.title: Earlier Warnings
n0054.gist: Later technological ease of large-scale testing, a bigger and more diverse research community, and decades-old warnings from scholars like Meehl and Kahneman explain why old concerns finally erupted into a crisis.

n0058.title: Psychology Replication Studies
n0058.gist: Large coordinated replication projects in psychology found that only about a third to half of classic findings reproduced, with effect sizes shrinking sharply and little support for sample differences as the cause.

n0064.title: Medicine and Cancer Biology
n0064.gist: Studies of highly cited medical and cancer research found replication rates as low as 11 to 44 percent, with effect sizes often far smaller than originally reported.

n0068.title: In Other Disciplines
n0068.gist: Low replication rates and poor reporting standards extend well beyond psychology, turning up in nutrition science, economics, water management, and new research involving large language models.
n0068.question: In other disciplines — does the crisis reach beyond psychology and medicine? (four field case studies)

n0069.title: Nutrition and Economics
n0069.gist: Nearly every common food ingredient has a study linking it to cancer risk, while economics replication attempts succeed only about 60 percent of the time with inflated original effect sizes.

n0076.title: Water Resource Management
n0076.gist: A 2019 analysis of nearly 2,000 water-management articles estimated that under 7 percent could even in principle be reproduced, mainly because papers omitted the information needed to redo them.

n0080.title: Large Language Model Research
n0080.gist: Research on and using large language models faces its own reproducibility threats, since closed commercial models change without notice, outputs vary run to run, and key methodological details often go unreported.

n0087.title: Survey Evidence Across Fields
n0087.gist: Large surveys find most scientists have failed to reproduce someone else's results, that unreplicable papers get cited more rather than less, and that half of thousands of recent social-science papers failed to replicate.

n0092.title: Causes: History and Publication System
n0092.gist: The crisis traces partly to science's runaway growth and commercialization, and partly to a publishing system that rewards positive, significant results over careful, reported-in-full ones.
n0092.question: Replication crisis — why does the system itself produce unreliable results? (historical and structural causes)

n0093.title: Historical and Sociological Causes
n0093.gist: Science's exponential growth, its commercialization through corporate-funded research, and confusion between the codes of science, media, and profit may have eroded quality control over decades.

n0101.title: Problems with the Publication System
n0101.gist: Journals overwhelmingly publish positive results, leaving negative findings in a 'file drawer,' which inflates the apparent rate of true discoveries and biases the published literature toward false positives.
n0101.sourceHeading: Problems with the publication system in science

n0108.title: Mathematical Errors
n0108.gist: Even top journals contain frequent statistical errors, such as mismatched p-values or wrongly testing whether one effect differs from another rather than testing the difference directly.

n0113.title: Publish or Perish Culture
n0113.gist: Career pressure to publish frequently pushes researchers toward strategies that make results look publishable rather than valid, discouraging the unglamorous but necessary work of replication.

n0120.title: Standards of Reporting
n0120.gist: Many papers omit the experimental details needed to redo them, and cognitive biases about whether a null result reflects a bad instrument or a bad theory let non-replicable findings accumulate unnoticed.

n0126.title: Questionable Practices and Statistical Issues
n0126.gist: Flexible research choices, from selective reporting to outright fraud, combined with chronically underpowered studies and shaky meta-analyses, make many positive findings statistically unreliable.
n0126.question: Replication crisis — what specific research and statistical practices generate false positives? (several mechanisms examined)

n0127.title: Questionable Research Practices
n0127.gist: Exploiting flexibility in data collection, analysis, and reporting, such as HARKing or selective reporting, is common across psychology and machine learning and inflates false-positive rates, sometimes shading into outright fraud.

n0138.title: Low Statistical Power
n0138.gist: Psychology, neuroscience, and economics studies typically have statistical power far below the 80 percent considered adequate, meaning a positive finding is unlikely to replicate even if it reflects a real effect.

n0147.title: Positive Effect Size Bias
n0147.gist: Underpowered studies systematically distort estimated effect sizes, usually inflating them when samples are small, which is why replications almost always find smaller effects than the original.

n0153.title: Problems of Meta-analysis
n0153.gist: Meta-analysis has its own flaws, since methods like the fail-safe number for unpublished null results can be miscalculated, and a single bad study can distort an entire pooled estimate.

n0171.title: Statistical Heterogeneity
n0171.gist: Much of the failure to replicate stems not from error but from genuine variation in true effect sizes across contexts, a heterogeneity so large in psychology that even exact replications often disagree.

n0178.title: Context, Bayesian, and NHST Critiques
n0178.gist: Some failures to replicate reflect genuine sensitivity to context, Bayesian reasoning shows that a significant result rarely guarantees future replication, and the entire logic of null-hypothesis testing may be unsuited to complex fields like social psychology, yet public trust in science has largely held.
n0178.question: Replication crisis — are failed replications inherent to how certain sciences test hypotheses? (several theoretical critiques)

n0179.title: Context Sensitivity
n0179.gist: Psychological effects often depend heavily on hidden contextual factors, and studies that re-coded the Reproducibility Project data found that higher context sensitivity strongly predicted lower replication success.

n0184.title: Bayesian Explanation
n0184.gist: Using Bayes' theorem shows that rejecting the null hypothesis at the common 5 percent threshold does not make the alternative 95 percent probable, and when the alternative is a priori unlikely, replication probability can be quite low.

n0192.title: Problem with Null Hypothesis Testing
n0192.gist: In complex fields like social psychology, where everything correlates a little, rejecting the null hypothesis barely supports any specific alternative, so a surplus of untested theories can accumulate without real evidence.

n0205.title: Public Awareness and Academic Response
n0205.gist: Most members of the public remain unaware of replication failures and still trust science's self-correction, even as the crisis provoked sharp, sometimes personal, disputes among researchers over how to respond.

n0219.title: Reform in Scientific Publishing
n0219.gist: Proposed fixes include clearer reporting standards, pre-registering studies before seeing results, stricter significance thresholds, better handling of p-values, and larger sample sizes.
n0219.question: Replication crisis — what publishing and statistical reforms could make results more trustworthy? (several proposed fixes)

n0220.title: Presentation of Methodology
n0220.gist: Poor reporting of experimental and statistical methods is widely blamed for the crisis, prompting calls for cultural change in how journals and funders demand transparency about design and analysis.

n0228.title: Result-Blind Peer Review
n0228.gist: Over 140 psychology journals now accept studies based on methodological rigor before results are known, a practice that has produced a far higher share of reported null results than earlier research.

n0232.title: Pre-registration of Studies
n0232.gist: Registered reports require researchers to lock in their methods and analysis plan before collecting data, which guarantees publication regardless of outcome and discourages after-the-fact data tweaking.

n0237.title: Metadata and Tracking Tools
n0237.gist: Proposed digital tools would track how often studies have been replicated and whether findings held up, letting journals, reviewers, or readers rate reproducibility directly.
n0237.sourceHeading: Metadata and digital tools for tracking replications

n0241.title: Requiring Smaller P-values
n0241.gist: A widely signed proposal to lower the significance threshold from 0.005 to 0.05 promised fewer false positives, but a follow-up study found neither that nor rival case-by-case recommendations were actually adopted in practice.

n0246.title: Addressing Misinterpretation of P-values
n0246.gist: Statisticians agree p-values are weaker evidence than commonly assumed, and some propose reporting an accompanying false-positive risk, calculated by working backward from an assumed prior probability, instead of labeling results simply significant or not.

n0252.title: Encouraging Larger Sample Sizes
n0252.gist: Because small samples and significance filtering inflate reported effect sizes, replications typically need larger samples, and techniques like cross-validation can curb overfitting without wasting data.

n0258.title: Replication Efforts and Collaboration
n0258.gist: Funders, universities, and large multi-lab collaborations have begun pooling money, training, and data across countries to systematically test whether findings generalize.
n0258.question: Replication efforts — what concrete institutional steps are being taken to replicate more research? (funding, training, databases)

n0259.title: Funding Replication
n0259.gist: Government agencies and private foundations have committed millions of dollars to fund replication studies and new institutes devoted to improving scientific research methods.

n0264.title: Education Reform
n0264.gist: Some university methods courses now have students attempt replications rather than original studies, and some recommend graduate students complete a replication before graduating.

n0268.title: Replication Databases
n0268.gist: Concern about wasted effort from uncoordinated replication attempts has led to new databases tracking replication studies across disciplines, alongside calls for undergraduate theses to include replication work.

n0275.title: Involving Original Authors
n0275.gist: Some argue original authors should join replication efforts since published methods are often too vague, and data show replications succeed far more often, 92 versus 65 percent, when original authors are involved.

n0280.title: Broader Changes and Open Science
n0280.gist: Beyond better statistics, some argue science needs triangulation across methods, models that treat psychological variables as context-dependent, theory-revising replication, and open data to truly fix the crisis.
n0280.question: Replication crisis — what deeper conceptual shifts, beyond procedural fixes, might resolve it? (several proposals)

n0281.title: Emphasize Triangulation, Not Just Replication
n0281.gist: Researchers argue that relying on replication alone can falsely reassure, and that combining independent methods with different weaknesses, called triangulation, better protects against flawed conclusions.

n0288.title: Complex Systems Paradigm
n0288.gist: Some argue psychology's standard linear causal model wrongly assumes stable, independent variables, and that treating mental variables as interdependent and context-adapting better explains why replications fail.

n0294.title: Replication Should Seek to Revise Theories
n0294.gist: Replication alone cannot resolve the crisis; efforts should also prune and strengthen theories, since reproducible findings best predict whether results generalize across contexts and time.
n0294.sourceHeading: Replication should seek to revise theories

n0298.title: Open Data and Open Science
n0298.gist: Open data, open-source software, and public repositories like the Open Science Framework aim to make analyses verifiable, though sophisticated researchers who share data may paradoxically face more scrutiny and criticism.

n0302.title: See Also and References
n0302.gist: A list of related statistical and methodological concepts and the cited sources underlying the article's claims.
